title: Appendix B: Three Classic Designs

sections.title: Choosing Between Push, Pull, and Both
What the Designs Have in Common

html:
Appendix B: Three Classic Designs

You can draw a URL shortener in a minute: an API, a database, and a redirect. Now imagine a popular link being shared during a live event. How many redirects can your first deployment handle before customers start waiting? If someone submits the same create-link request twice, do you issue two short codes or return the one you already made? And if the database commits a link but the response never reaches the caller, how will you find it again?

A social timeline and a notification service raise different questions. A timeline can show slightly older posts for some readers, but it must not accidentally reveal a private post. A notification can arrive late, but sending the same payment reminder six times can be worse than sending it once an hour late. Those requirements change the design before we choose a database, a queue, or a cache.

We’ll work through these systems one request at a time. First, decide what the person using the service should experience. Then estimate the load and find the resource most likely to run out. Finally, interrupt an operation partway through and decide what the next request should do. The example numbers can change. What matters is whether they tell you when to add capacity, cap a queue, or refuse new work.

The listings come in two kinds. Listings B.1, B.2, and B.6 are self-contained and were run, and the numbers quoted in the text come from those runs. The insert in Listing B.3 was exercised against SQLite. The others assume helper objects such as a cache client and a message queue, so they show only the logic needed for the design discussion. None of them is production code: error handling, configuration, and metrics are left out so that the calculation can be checked alongside the design.

A Method for Any Design

Start with what someone using the service needs to happen. Then follow one request through every system it touches. At each boundary, ask who owns the data, what the caller can know after a timeout, and which resource the next step will occupy. A diagram becomes useful when it makes those answers visible.

  1. What does the service promise? State it as something a customer experiences. “A short link redirects to the right page” is a promise. “We have a cache” is not.

  2. How big is the workload? Convert rates, durations, and sizes into concurrency and storage, using the arithmetic from Chapters 1 and 2. Use the peak as well as the average, because the peak determines whether capacity runs out.

  3. Which resource reaches its limit first under the intended workload, and what limits the work admitted to it?

  4. Who owns each piece of data, what identifies an operation across retries, and what happens to an operation whose outcome we cannot confirm?

  5. What happens when each dependency is slow, unavailable, or wrong, and has anyone tried the fallback?

  6. What would the on-call engineer look at to know the promise is being kept, and what should they do when it is not?

Use the questions to find the decision that could change the design. For the shortener, redirect volume tells us when a single read path may run out of capacity. For notifications, the harder question may be what a worker does after it sends a message and crashes before recording success. That failure requires an operation identity and a recovery rule even if the traffic fits on one machine.

When time is limited, write down the contract and the likely failure first. Draw enough architecture to follow the request and test the assumption. Add components only when the evidence or the product’s promise calls for them.

Doing the Arithmetic in Code

Capacity estimates are easier to audit when each assumption appears next to the calculation that uses it. A short script also makes it possible to compare traffic and retention scenarios without repeating the arithmetic by hand. Listing \(\ref{lst:estimator}\) reproduces the shortener and timeline estimates used below.

[
  language=Python,
  label={lst:estimator},
  caption={A back-of-envelope estimator. Changing an assumption changes every number that depends on it.}]
SECONDS_PER_DAY = 86_400
SECONDS_PER_MONTH = 30 * SECONDS_PER_DAY          # 2,592,000

def shortener(creations_per_month=50e6, reads_per_link=100,
              peak_factor=5, years=5, bytes_per_link=500):
    creations = creations_per_month / SECONDS_PER_MONTH
    redirects = creations * reads_per_link
    links = creations_per_month * 12 * years
    return {
        "creations/s": creations,                  # 19.3
        "redirects/s average": redirects,          # 1,929
        "redirects/s peak": redirects * peak_factor,   # 9,645
        "storage, TB": links * bytes_per_link / 1e12,  # 1.5
        "code space used, %": 100 * links / 62 ** 7,   # 0.085
    }

def timeline(users=20e6, posts_per_user=2, opens_per_user=10,
             followers=200):
    posts = users * posts_per_user / SECONDS_PER_DAY
    reads = users * opens_per_user / SECONDS_PER_DAY
    fanout = posts * followers
    return {"posts/s": posts, "reads/s": reads,
            "inserts/s": fanout,
            "write:read ratio": fanout / reads,
            "seconds to fan out 10M followers": 10e6 / fanout}

A URL Shortener

What the Service Promises

Given a short code, the service sends the visitor to the destination the creator chose, quickly, for as long as the link is active. Two consequences of that sentence matter more than they first appear. A link that has been disabled, because it was abusive or its owner deleted it, has to stop redirecting within a bounded time. And a code, once issued, must never point somewhere else.

Sizing the Service

Suppose the service creates 50 million links a month and receives about 100 redirects for every link created.

Estimates for the URL shortener. The \(5\times\) peak factor and the 500-byte record size are assumptions to replace with measurements.
Quantity Value Derivation
Creations, average 19/s \(50\times10^{6} \div 2.59\times10^{6}\) s
Redirects, average 1,930/s \(19.3 \times 100\)
Redirects, peak \(\approx\) 9,600/s assumed \(5\times\) average
Links after 5 years \(3\times10^{9}\) \(50\times10^{6}\times 60\)
Storage \(\approx\) 1.5 TB \(3\times10^{9}\times 500\) B
Code space, 7 characters, base 62 \(3.5\times10^{12}\) \(62^{7}\)

Seven base-62 characters provide about \(3.5\times10^{12}\) codes, and five years of creations would use about 0.085 percent of that space. This leaves room to choose between allocation schemes, although random allocation still requires collision handling. The estimated creation rate is about 19 per second, compared with 1,930 redirects per second. Test the combined workload, including administrative updates, before choosing the database size.

Where Capacity Runs Out

The first capacity test should target peak cache misses. The store must handle the redirects that the cache cannot answer, including a cold-cache recovery interval. If the cache answers 90 percent of redirects, the database receives about 960 lookups per second at the 9,600 peak, which one primary or replica must demonstrate in a workload test. At a 50 percent hit rate it receives 4,800, and that higher rate needs its own capacity test. The hit rate is therefore an assumption the whole design rests on, and it belongs in the hidden-assumptions review with a measurement and a threshold, as Chapter 5 treated it.

Generating Short Codes

Creation needs a code that no earlier creation has used, and there are four approaches to compare. Each fails differently, so Table \(\ref{tab:appb-codes}\) lays them side by side before we choose.

The fourth approach works well here. Each creation instance leases a block of identifiers, say 10,000, from a central allocator and hands them out locally. With four creation instances, each contacts the allocator about once every half hour at this rate. Before a number becomes a code, it passes through a small permutation, so that sequential counters produce codes that look unrelated. Listing \(\ref{lst:scramble}\) shows one way to do it.

[
  language=Python,
  label={lst:scramble},
  caption={A permutation of the counter, then base-62 encoding. Distinct counters always give distinct codes.}]
import hashlib

ALPHABET = ("0123456789"
            "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
            "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz")
CODE_LENGTH = 7
SPACE = 62 ** CODE_LENGTH   # 3,521,614,606,208 codes
HALF_BITS = 21              # 2**42, above SPACE
MASK = (1 << HALF_BITS) - 1

def _round(value, key, round_no):
    data = f"{key}:{round_no}:{value}".encode()
    digest = hashlib.sha256(data).digest()
    return int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "big") & MASK

def _feistel(n, key, rounds=4):
    left, right = n >> HALF_BITS, n & MASK
    for r in range(rounds):
        left, right = right, left ^ _round(right, key, r)
    return (left << HALF_BITS) | right

def scramble(counter, key):
    """Map a counter below SPACE to a distinct value."""
    n = _feistel(counter, key)
    while n >= SPACE:       # cycle walking, until in range
        n = _feistel(n, key)
    return n

def encode(n):
    chars = []
    for _ in range(CODE_LENGTH):
        n, digit = divmod(n, 62)
        chars.append(ALPHABET[digit])
    return "".join(reversed(chars))

The permutation uses a Feistel network. It splits a number into two halves and repeatedly mixes one half into the other. The construction is a permutation regardless of the mixing function, which ensures that distinct inputs produce distinct outputs. The catch is that its range is a power of two, here \(2^{42}\), and our code space is \(62^7\), which is smaller. The loop is what handles the mismatch. If a result falls outside the code space, we apply the permutation again, and we keep going until it lands inside. This is called cycle walking, and because \(2^{42}\) is only 1.25 times larger than \(62^7\), a near-uniform permutation needs about 1.25 passes on average. Roughly 20 percent of first results fall outside the code space. Running the code over the first million counters produced a million distinct seven-character codes.

The permutation obscures the relationship between sequential identifiers, which makes adjacent codes harder to recognize by inspection. It provides no cryptographic protection against systematic guessing or enumeration. If the service requires unpredictable codes, generate them using a cryptographically secure random generator and enforce uniqueness in the database, or adopt a vetted format-preserving cipher. This illustrative Feistel construction must not be used as a security control.

The uniqueness guarantee itself comes from the database, not from the allocator. The link table enforces a unique constraint on the code, so a bug in the allocator shows up as a rejected write instead of a visitor sent to the wrong page. Creation requests include an operation identifier supplied by the client, so a retry after a timeout returns the code already issued instead of minting a second one. That is the idea behind the payment operation in Chapter 3, applied to a far cheaper operation. Listing \(\ref{lst:create}\) shows both guarantees.

[
  language=SQL,
  label={lst:create},
  caption={The schema, the block lease, and an idempotent create.}]
CREATE TABLE links (
    code          CHAR(7)     PRIMARY KEY,
    destination   TEXT        NOT NULL,
    owner_id      BIGINT      NOT NULL,
    operation_id  UUID        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    disabled_at   TIMESTAMPTZ
);

-- Lease 10,000 identifiers. Each creation instance runs
-- this about twice an hour. The single row is the only
-- shared counter.
UPDATE id_allocator
   SET next_value = next_value + 10000
 RETURNING next_value - 10000 AS block_start;

-- Create a link. A retry with the same operation_id
-- inserts nothing.
INSERT INTO links (code, destination, owner_id, operation_id)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4)
ON CONFLICT (operation_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING code;
-- If no row came back, this was a retry:
--   SELECT code FROM links WHERE operation_id = $4;

If the insert returns nothing, the request was a repeat, and a second query returns the original code. The counter value taken for the repeat is unused, and the code space allows those gaps. The other direction of the logic is the redirect, where the rules from Chapter 5 apply. A miss is loaded once under request coalescing, a confirmed absence is cached briefly, and a timeout is never mistaken for absence (Listing \(\ref{lst:resolve}\)).

[
  language=Python,
  label={lst:resolve},
  caption={The redirect lookup. Only a positive answer that the code does not exist is cached as absent.}]
MISSING = object()

def resolve(code):
    key = f"link:{code}"
    value = cache.get(key)
    if value is not None:
        return None if value is MISSING else value
    with single_flight(key):            # one loader per key
        # Re-check after waiting for the loader.
        value = cache.get(key)
        if value is not None:
            return None if value is MISSING else value
        row = db.fetch_one(             # timeout: raises
            "SELECT destination FROM links "
            "WHERE code = %s AND disabled_at IS NULL",
            (code,))
        if row is None:
            # Confirmed absence, kept briefly.
            cache.set(key, MISSING, ttl=30)
            return None
        # Jitter spreads expiry.
        ttl = 300 + random.randint(0, 60)
        cache.set(key, row.destination, ttl=ttl)
        return row.destination

The jitter on the lifetime spreads expiry so that entries written together do not all expire together, the same precaution as in Chapter 5.

How the Shortener Fails

A permanent redirect (HTTP status 301) permits caching that can bypass the service on later visits, which affects revocation and click counts. For revocable links in this design, return a temporary redirect (302 or 307) with explicit cache controls such as Cache-Control: no-store. The response status alone does not prevent caching. Test browser and intermediary behavior against the required disable delay.

Disabling a link raises a related problem. Deleting the row does nothing about copies already in the cache, so the link service has to define how long a disabled link may keep redirecting. If the answer is “as long as the cache lifetime,” then that lifetime is a product decision with consequences for abuse response, and if it is too long, the disable path must also invalidate the cached entry.

Bots add a third kind of trouble by probing random codes. Every unknown code is a cache miss that reaches the database, and the short negative entry in Listing \(\ref{lst:resolve}\) absorbs most of it. After a cache failure, the full peak lands on the store. At 9,600 lookups per second and a 5 ms lookup, about 48 are in flight on average, which a pool sized for the steady state will not hold. The recovery plan is the one from Chapter 5: bound the database’s concurrency, serve a small warm set first, and let the cache refill through request coalescing.

Clicks are counted through a queue, and the delivery guarantee can be chosen honestly. A small undercount is acceptable, and a redirect that waits for the count is not. At-least-once delivery with counts described as approximate does the job. Abuse needs its own path as well. Destinations are scanned after creation rather than during it, and a finding feeds the same disable mechanism. Creation is also the cheapest place to stop abuse, so it is where per-account rate limits belong.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & At least 90 percent of redirects are answered from the cache, so the link store receives fewer than 1,
000 lookups per second at peak.

Condition that tests it & Cache loss, campaign traffic, or repeated scans change the miss rate.
Constraint or invariant & Bound store-read concurrency during ordinary misses and recovery after cache loss.
Evidence and uncertainty & Estimated from a \(5\times\) peak factor and an assumed popularity skew. Not yet measured against real traffic.

Hit rate during campaigns, after cache loss, and under scanning. Whether the store’s read capacity covers a 50 percent hit rate.
Signal and evaluation window & Observe hit rate and store lookup rate over the stated ten-minute window.
Control and decision & If the hit rate stays below 80 percent for ten minutes, add negative caching or read capacity before peak.
Owner and review trigger & The redirect-service owner, who also owns the disable-propagation time objective. Review after each failure drill and before increasing traffic.
:::

A Social Timeline

What the Timeline Promises

When a customer opens the app, it shows recent posts from the accounts they follow, newest first, within the product’s response-time target. Every returned post must satisfy the customer’s access permissions. That last clause turns the problem from one of speed into one of correctness, and it will come back in a later subsection.

Sizing the Timeline

Suppose 20 million daily users. Each posts twice a day, opens the timeline ten times a day, and the authors of these posts have 200 followers on average, weighted by how often each author posts. An average across accounts alone would underestimate fan-out work if popular accounts post more frequently.

Reads outnumber posts five to one, which suggests a read-heavy system. The workload changes once the application materializes timelines at write time. If every new post is copied into each follower’s stored timeline at the moment it is written, a practice called fan-out on write, each post becomes about 200 inserts. Timeline inserts then occur at roughly forty times the rate of timeline reads. This design shifts the cost to writes. We pay at write time, in bulk, so that each read becomes a single lookup.

The Fan-Out Bottleneck

The scarce resource is fan-out throughput, and the danger is what happens when a very large account posts. At 92,600 inserts per second, ten million follower inserts consume about 108 seconds of the fleet’s entire throughput, before ordinary posts are counted. If that job monopolizes a FIFO worker queue, ordinary posts wait behind it. Chunking and fair scheduling reduce that delay, but the ten million writes still have to be completed. Chapter 12 named this problem head-of-line blocking: one item at the front of an ordered line holds up everything behind it.

Choosing Between Push, Pull, and Both

For ordinary accounts, a worker appends the post’s identifier to each follower’s stored timeline. Above a follower threshold, say several hundred thousand, the post skips fan-out and is recorded only in the author’s own list. When a customer opens the app, the feed service takes their precomputed timeline, pulls recent posts from the few large accounts they follow, merges the two by time, and loads the post bodies by identifier.

The threshold should come from measurement. Below it the read path is cheap and the write path pays, and above it the write path is protected and the read path pays, in proportion to how many large accounts the reader follows. A cap on how many large accounts one read will merge belongs in the design from the start, since without one the read path has no upper bound.

The Write and Read Paths

The timeline stores post identifiers, not posts, and the choice of structure makes a replay harmless. Adding a member to a sorted set with the creation time as its score is idempotent. A worker that crashes and replays its batch writes the same member with the same score, and nothing changes. We design toward that property wherever we can: choose a stored representation in which replaying a message changes nothing (Listing \(\ref{lst:fanout}\)).

[
  language=Python,
  label={lst:fanout},
  caption={Fan-out on write into sorted sets, and the read path that merges and filters.}]
TIMELINE_LENGTH = 800

def fan_out(post_id, created_ms, follower_ids):
    pipe = redis.pipeline(transaction=False)
    for follower in follower_ids:
        key = f"timeline:{follower}"
        # Same member and score: a replay changes nothing.
        pipe.zadd(key, {post_id: created_ms})
        # Keep only the newest 800 entries.
        pipe.zremrangebyrank(key, 0, -(TIMELINE_LENGTH + 1))
    pipe.execute()

def read_timeline(viewer_id, limit=50):
    key = f"timeline:{viewer_id}"
    entries = redis.zrevrange(
        key, 0, 2 * limit - 1, withscores=True)
    for author in large_accounts(viewer_id)[:MAX_PULLED]:
        # Pulled at read time.
        entries += recent_posts(author, limit)
    entries.sort(key=lambda e: e[1], reverse=True)
    ids = [post_id for post_id, _ in entries]
    # The post store applies this viewer's visibility rules.
    return post_store.load_visible(viewer_id, ids, limit)

The trim on every insert keeps each timeline at 800 entries, which is where the 128 GB storage estimate came from. The final read step rechecks visibility because fan-out may have stored a post before the viewer lost permission to read it. The next subsection covers that case.

Visibility and Deletion

Permission changes affect timelines that were already written. Suppose a customer blocks someone, a post is deleted, or an account goes private. The stored timelines already contain identifiers the reader should no longer see. If permissions were checked only at fan-out time, we would be enforcing a decision made hours ago. So the read path checks visibility again, against the authoritative source, when it loads each post. The stored timeline is a hint about what might be shown, and the post store decides what may be shown.

Deletion works the same way. A deleted post leaves a tombstone, a marker saying the item is gone, and readers skip tombstoned identifiers. A background job removes the stale identifiers from timelines later, and nothing the customer sees waits for it.

How the Timeline Fails

The right measure of freshness is the delay between a post being accepted and its appearing in a follower’s timeline, at the 95th and 99th percentile. A queue depth of a million means little without the rate, so alerts should watch the age of the oldest unprocessed post, and separate queues or priorities should keep a large account from delaying ordinary ones.

A new user, or one whose stored timeline was evicted, has nothing to read. The timeline can be rebuilt from the authors they follow, under a concurrency limit, serving a reduced version first. Without the limit, a cache flush becomes a database outage, the same pattern as the cold-cache failures of Chapter 5.

Reading has its own amplification. A reader who follows 300 large accounts triggers 300 pulls on every timeline load. The cap on merged accounts bounds that cost, and the merge rule has to specify which accounts are included when the cap applies.

Follow and unfollow need a decision too. Following someone does not put their older posts into your stored timeline unless the design says it does. We decide which, write it down, and test that unfollowing removes their posts from the next read rather than merely the next fan-out.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & The fan-out fleet, sized for the average insert rate, stays within a freshness objective because very large accounts bypass fan-out.
Condition that tests it & A high-follower account posts during peak demand, or a reader follows many large accounts.
Constraint or invariant & Bound work per fan-out batch and high-follower account pulls per read. Enforce visibility checks at read time.
Evidence and uncertainty & Derived from 463 posts per second and 200 average followers. The follower distribution is assumed, not measured.

The right follower threshold, the number of large accounts a typical reader follows, and behavior during a real surge.
Signal and evaluation window & Observe post-to-visible delay, oldest fan-out job, and pulls per read over two consecutive configured evaluation windows.
Control and decision & Lower the threshold when post-to-visible delay exceeds the objective for two consecutive windows.
Owner and review trigger & The feed team owns freshness. The post-store owner owns visibility rules, and the read path must call them. Review after each failure drill and before increasing traffic.
:::

A Notification Service

What Each Message Promises

The service delivers the right message to the right person through the channel they chose, once, in time for it to be useful. Every clause rules out a failure: wrong message, wrong person, wrong channel, duplicate, late. The consequence depends on the message. A one-time passcode that arrives too late is effectively lost. For a marketing message, a duplicate is an annoyance and a lost one goes unnoticed. The two kinds of message have different promises, which is a first hint that they should not share a queue.

Sizing the Service

Suppose 10 million notifications go out on an ordinary day, and a campaign adds 2 million more over ten minutes. The email provider accepts 1,000 messages per second for this account.

Estimates for the notification service. The drain time assumes the campaign has the whole provider allowance.
Quantity Value Derivation
Ordinary day, average 116/s \(10^{7}\div 86{,}400\)
Campaign rate 3,333/s \(2\times10^{6}\div 600\)
Provider limit 1,000/s assumed contract
Campaign drain time \(\approx\) 33 min \(2\times10^{6}\div 1{,}000\)

The Provider’s Limit

What runs out first is the provider’s rate limit, which everything the service sends must share. At campaign speed, demand is more than three times the allowance. If campaign mail and a login passcode share one queue and one allowance, a code-generation request can wait behind up to half an hour of marketing. The arithmetic makes the architectural argument before anyone draws a diagram.

Separating Message Classes

Each class of message gets its own queue and its own delivery deadline, and all classes draw on one allowance. The mechanism that keeps campaigns from starving passcodes is a token bucket that holds back its last tokens for priority traffic. Transactional messages may take any token. Bulk messages may take a token only if enough remain to leave the reserve untouched (Listing \(\ref{lst:bucket}\)).

[
  language=Python,
  label={lst:bucket},
  caption={One allowance with a reserve. Priority traffic may use the reserve when tokens are available; bulk traffic must leave it untouched.}]
import time

class ReserveBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, capacity, reserve,
                 clock=time.monotonic):
        self.rate = rate
        self.capacity, self.reserve = capacity, reserve
        self.tokens, self.clock = capacity, clock
        self.stamp = clock()

    def _refill(self):
        now = self.clock()
        earned = (now - self.stamp) * self.rate
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity, self.tokens + earned)
        self.stamp = now

    def try_take(self, priority):
        self._refill()
        floor = 0 if priority else self.reserve
        if self.tokens - 1 >= floor:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

This version is not thread-safe, and a real one needs a lock or an atomic operation in a shared store, which also means deciding what happens to the allowance if that store fails over (Chapter 14). The priority reserve needs a workload test. With a rate of 1,000 per second, a bucket capacity of 1,000, reserve of 300, transactional traffic at 100 per second, and a campaign offering 3,333 per second, a simulation admitted every transactional message and about 900 campaign messages per second. The campaign therefore takes about 37 minutes to drain, not 33, because the transactional traffic takes its share first. The reserve also acts as a burst cushion. When bulk traffic has drained the bucket to its floor, a burst of 400 transactional messages finds 300 tokens waiting and then continues at the refill rate.

Every message includes an operation identifier assigned when the request is accepted, a class, and an expiry. The worker checks the expiry before sending. A passcode that is valid for five minutes and has waited six is dropped and recorded as expired, not sent late (Listing \(\ref{lst:deliver}\)).

Duplicates, Losses, and Preferences

The hard case is the payment timeout from Chapter 3 again. A worker submits the message, but the provider call times out before the worker receives a result. If the provider supports an idempotency key with a sufficient retention period, the worker resubmits the same operation identifier under that contract. Otherwise, it must determine whether the original submission could still succeed. A negative status lookup is conclusive only when the provider documents the lookup scope and a completion bound for the earlier request, as Chapter 3 explains. When the provider cannot establish the outcome, the notification policy must choose between possible duplication and possible loss. For a login passcode, retrying may be preferable to blocking login, but duplicate messages can still confuse customers and trigger provider rate limits. A receipt should use the provider’s status lookup, if there is one, before resending. A marketing message can usually be allowed to go missing.

[
  language=Python,
  label={lst:deliver},
  caption={The send path. The checks that depend on time and preference run at send time, not at acceptance.}]
def deliver(msg):
    now = clock.now()
    if now > msg.expires_at:
        return record(msg, "EXPIRED")
    if not preferences.allows(msg.recipient, msg.channel,
                              msg.kind, now):
        # Opted out, or inside quiet hours.
        return record(msg, "SUPPRESSED")
    priority = msg.klass == "transactional"
    if not allowance.try_take(priority=priority):
        return requeue(msg, delay=backoff(msg.attempts))
    record(msg, "ATTEMPTING")       # durable intent first
    try:
        ref = provider.send(msg, timeout=2.0,
                            idempotency_key=msg.operation_id)
    except Timeout:
        return record(msg, "UNKNOWN")   # resolved later
    return record(msg, "ACCEPTED", provider_ref=ref)

The two checks at the top are the preference rule. A customer who unsubscribes at 9:00 must not receive a campaign message that was accepted at 8:00 and dequeued at 9:05, so the worker looks at the current preference and quiet hours at send time. The state names at the bottom are the precise vocabulary. “Accepted by the provider” is not “delivered,” and neither is “opened.” Record which of these each status means and report them separately. Delivery receipts often arrive late, so any report built from them should state its lag. Recording the attempt before calling the provider is what lets another worker pick up an UNKNOWN message after a crash.

How the Notification Service Fails

When the provider is down, queues grow, and the expiry rule bounds them: expired passcodes are discarded instead of being sent after they can no longer be used. A second channel for transactional messages, such as text messages when email is down, is a reasonable fallback. It brings its own allowance and its own evidence of delivery, though, and it needs its own test before anyone relies on it.

A retry policy that resends on every timeout multiplies load on a provider that is already slow, so exactly one component owns retries, with a budget and a backoff (Chapter 4). Malformed templates and invalid addresses fail every time. After a bounded number of attempts they move to a quarantine with an owner (Chapter 12), and the queue keeps moving.

Finally, every team in the company wants to send notifications; without per-producer quotas, one buggy producer can use the whole allowance. The quota belongs at acceptance, where rejecting a request is cheap.

::: hiddenassumptions

Assumption and scope & Reserving part of the provider allowance for transactional messages keeps their delay within the delivery objective while a campaign runs.
Condition that tests it & A campaign burst overlaps transactional messages or the provider slows.
Constraint or invariant & All producers and message classes share the provider allowance. Apply expiry and preference checks before dispatch.
Evidence and uncertainty & Arithmetic and a simulation of one bucket: a 3

,
333 per second campaign against a 1,000 per second limit. No test yet with the real provider.

Whether the provider enforces its limit per second or per minute, how it counts retries, and whether it supports idempotency keys.

Signal and evaluation window & Measure queue age by message class and provider acceptance through the ten-minute campaign burst and its drain period.
Control and decision & Page when the age of the oldest transactional message exceeds the objective.
Owner and review trigger & The notification-platform team owns allocation. Each producing team owns its quota and its content. Review after each failure drill and before increasing traffic.
:::

What the Designs Have in Common

Putting the three designs side by side, the same moves show up in each.

The arithmetic named the constraint before we chose any component. For the shortener it was the cache hit rate, for the timeline it was fan-out throughput, and for the notification service it was a provider allowance we do not control. None of them was the database, which is where most whiteboard discussions begin.

Each design also protected one class of work from another. Campaigns cannot starve passcodes, celebrity posts cannot starve ordinary ones, and analytics cannot slow redirects. Every one of those protections is a reservation or a separate path, and each costs some utilization that we accepted on purpose.

Operations used the same identities across retries, and wherever we could arrange it the stored representation made a replay harmless. The dependency whose outcome can be unknown was named, and the class of message or request decided the policy for it. There was no single right answer, which is why the review records a decision and its reasons instead of a rule.

And the measure of success was never a component metric. It was disable-propagation time, post-to-visible delay, and the age of the oldest passcode, each stated in seconds and each something a customer would notice.

You can run the same six questions on a design you have never seen. We start with the promise, compute the numbers, find the resource that runs out, and ask what an operation’s identity is. The boxes and arrows can wait until the end.
